patients.label: 35-year-old man who survived out-of-hospital cardiac arrest with a Type 1 Brugada pattern at peak exercise stress testing

identity_evidence.quote: We describe a case of a young man who survived a cardiac arrest during physical exertion.
We report the case of a 35-year-old previously asymptomatic man who survived an out-of-hospital cardiac arrest

attribution_limitations: The Brugada syndrome diagnosis is described as assumed from the exercise test, while the abstract calls the exercise-induced Type 1 pattern diagnostic; the authors state a pharmacological provocation test was not performed.
The discussion says dual pathology (Brugada phenotype with idiopathic ventricular fibrillation) cannot be entirely excluded; the sentence does not itself name this patient.
Only one sibling is reported with a Type 1 pattern after family ajmaline testing; the number of relatives tested and results for the others are not given.

The abstract resting ECG is not stated to be the same recording as the admission ECG or the high right precordial lead ECG; the heart-rate range at peak exercise and the 186 b.p.m. caption value are separate statements.

Figure 1
Admission electrocardiogram showing incomplete right branch block with normal QT interval.

Figure 2
Modified electrocardiogram with high right precordial leads showing incomplete right bundle branch block with ST-segment elevation of 1 mm, with no record of Type 1 Brugada pattern (V1–V2 corresponds to V1–V2 on the second intercostal space, V3–V4 on the third intercostal space,and V5–V6 on the fourth intercostal space).

Figure 3
Electrocardiogram results on exercise stress test. (A) Baseline modified electrocardiogram with high right precordial lead. (B) Maximum ST-segment augmentation with transition to the Type 1 pattern (circle) occurring during peak exercise at a heart rate of 186 b.p.m. (C) Electrocardiograms representing termination of testing at 5 min into recovery.

Electrocardiogram results on exercise stress test. (A) Baseline modified electrocardiogram with high right precordial lead. limitations: Single-case report with no tables or supplements; discussion sentences about published series and guidelines were treated as background, not patient facts.
The graphical abstract and the uncaptioned inline graphic have no source link to the patient and are left unresolved; pixels are reviewed in the separate visual target.
No dates or ages are given for events before the 12-month follow-up, so only the ordering stated in the text (ICD implanted after the genetic panel) is recorded.

claims.text: A treadmill exercise stress test with high right precordial leads, performed to reproduce the circumstances of the arrest and exclude catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia, documented intermittent electrical alternans with a Type 1 Brugada pattern at peak exercise, with ST-segment changes resolving gradually during recovery and no ventricular arrhythmias. An electrophysiology study was not pursued, an extended genetic panel was negative, and a subcutaneous ICD was subsequently implanted. The authors state the Brugada syndrome diagnosis was assumed on the basis of the exercise test.
